target: Agent 1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for millions.
objection: A federal holiday would not automatically solve the scheduling problem because private employers are not required to give paid time off. Many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other hourly service jobs would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday could widen inequities by helping workers with more flexibility while leaving constrained workers behind.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a federal holiday is ineffective because private employers may not provide paid leave, so low-income workers would still be stuck working.
objection: A holiday can be designed with enforceable voting-time protections, such as a federal requirement that employers provide guaranteed time to vote. Since that design would remove the wage-loss/working-time problem the objection relies on, the inequity criticism depends on an avoidable assumption that the policy is only symbolic.

target: Agent 1’s response that a holiday would materially reduce the scheduling barrier by giving workers more usable time to vote.
objection: Even if schools close and some workplaces shift, a federal holiday does not by itself change the central constraint for many low-income voters: whether their own employer gives them usable time away from work. Private employers can still schedule retail, food service, caregiving, and other essential workers, so the extra day may not become actual voting time for them.

target: Agent 2’s argument that a holiday mostly fails to create real time off for low-income workers.
objection: A national holiday changes the broader demand and logistics environment, not just the legal status of the date: schools and childcare close, consumer activity tends to fall, and many employers respond by reducing hours or closing. That makes it more likely that hourly workers will have usable non-working time to vote, so the assumption that most will still be stuck working is overstated.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully converts into non-working time for constrained workers.
objection: Although a holiday changes some calendars, it does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave. Many essential service and customer-facing businesses can remain open and keep scheduling hourly workers, so the holiday does not reliably produce real voting time for low-income workers and may mainly benefit workers with more flexible jobs.

target: Agent 2’s assumption that low-income workers will still largely lack usable time off under a holiday.
objection: A federal holiday changes everyday scheduling conditions, not just legal labels. Employers and workers commonly adjust to holiday status by reducing hours, closing, or staggering shifts, especially in retail and food service, so many hourly workers who would otherwise work normal hours are more likely to have off-duty time to vote.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a holiday will reliably shift ordinary work and school schedules enough to help constrained workers.
objection: Because a federal holiday does not require private employers to close or grant paid leave, many low-income hourly workplaces can stay open and schedule shifts as usual. That means the holiday’s effect on non-working time is uneven and depends on employer choice, so it is not a dependable fix for schedule barriers.

target: Agent 2’s claim that the policy mainly benefits flexible workers and leaves low-income workers unchanged.
objection: A national holiday changes the baseline scheduling environment for employers and workers. Many customer-facing businesses reduce hours or close because of lower demand and shifted public-school/transport calendars, so the holiday can convert into non-working time for a substantial share of hourly workers rather than leaving schedules essentially unchanged.

target: Agent 1’s repeated argument that a national holiday moves voting off the ordinary school/work calendar for the workers most constrained by schedules.
objection: Federal holidays do not compel private employers to close or provide paid leave, so workplaces employing many low-income hourly workers can remain open and still schedule employees. As a result, the holiday does not reliably translate into usable non-working time for those workers, and the tradeoff between lost wages and voting can remain.

target: Agent 1’s overall claim that Election Day as a holiday is an effective turnout-supporting reform.
objection: As a standalone reform, an Election Day holiday is not as effective at raising turnout as reforms that directly change voting access, such as automatic voter registration or enforceable state requirements for time off to vote. Holidays are only an indirect convenience measure, while the major barriers to turnout are better addressed by more direct access reforms.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday is only a symbolic or low-impact convenience measure.
objection: A holiday directly targets a major turnout barrier: Election Day falling on a normal school/work day compresses available time and can force people to miss work or school, lose wages, or make last-minute arrangements. By shifting schools and workplace operations, a holiday expands non-work time and can therefore raise turnout more than the objection suggests.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a holiday broadly expands usable non-work time for constrained workers.
objection: The key weak assumption is that low-income hourly workers will actually get the day off in practice. A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many retail, restaurant, caregiving, and similar workplaces can still schedule employees and leave those workers facing the same lost-wages-versus-voting tradeoff.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday is merely a weak nudge and not a meaningful turnout reform.
objection: A national holiday is not just a convenience nudge; it directly changes the practical time constraints that keep millions from voting. It gives voters more usable hours for polling and voting steps and reduces the need to miss work or school, so it can plausibly raise turnout among people whose main barrier is schedule control.

target: Agent 1’s claim that the holiday would broadly raise turnout by giving low-income workers usable time off.
objection: That causal chain depends on the assumption that a federal holiday actually gives most low-income hourly workers usable non-working time without wage loss. Since private employers are not required to close or pay workers, many shift workers may still have to choose between working and voting, so the holiday may mainly benefit people with more flexibility instead.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday is an ineffective turnout strategy because it only indirectly helps convenience.
objection: Election Day on a normal work/school day creates concrete time-budget barriers; a holiday changes those real conditions by expanding non-school, non-work time and reducing the need for paid leave or special arrangements. That makes the policy a direct access reform, not merely an abstract or symbolic gesture.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a national holiday would shift schools’ and employers’ operating conditions enough to reduce schedule barriers for hourly workers.
objection: The weak assumption is that the holiday would actually give low-income shift workers usable time off. A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so retail, restaurant, caregiving, and other customer-facing workplaces can remain open and keep employees on schedule, leaving the work-vote tradeoff intact.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday is only a small marginal convenience effect.
objection: A national holiday directly changes the real-world schedule conditions that constrain voting by moving Election Day off a normal work/school day. That expands non-work time for many voters and is consistent with broad public support and international practice, which suggests it can meaningfully improve access.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that the holiday broadly reduces time-budget pressure for the workers most constrained by schedules.
objection: A federal holiday is not a mandate on private employers, so many essential customer-facing workplaces can stay open and schedule shifts. For those workers, the holiday does not reliably create time to vote without losing wages, meaning the policy may not broadly reduce schedule barriers for the people who most need help.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday is only an indirect nudge and unlikely to meaningfully raise turnout.
objection: By changing school and work schedules on Election Day, a holiday directly reduces the time and wage costs of voting. It is therefore a substantive turnout-supporting reform rather than just a symbolic convenience, and its broad bipartisan support and use in many OECD countries indicate it is administratively workable.
